summary: Specifies how new MIME media types and subtypes get registered, answering open questions about the requirements and the administrative procedure. It is informational. It was replaced by RFC 2045, RFC 2046, RFC 2047, RFC 2048 and RFC 2049.

eli5.summary: When someone invents a new kind of file label, there has to be a way to put it on the official list. This explains the steps for doing that.

questions: how to register a mime media type
what is the x- prefix in mime types
subtitle: How new MIME media types get registered with IANA, and why the original rules were loosened.

tldr.problem: The original MIME registration rules were built for mail and were seen as too restrictive for wider use, which raised questions about requirements and procedure.
tldr.mechanism: Propose the type on a review mailing list, wait two weeks, then send it to IANA with a filled-in template. IANA registers it and assigns an OID.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1590 was replaced by RFC 2045, RFC 2046, RFC 2047, RFC 2048 and RFC 2049.

today: RFC 1590 is Informational and has been obsoleted by RFC 2045, RFC 2046, RFC 2047, RFC 2048 and RFC 2049. Use those for current MIME rules.

sections.title: Why the Procedure Was Revisited
sections.content:
RFC 1521 defined how to register new data types for MIME. The registry exists to make identifiers available and to prevent naming conflicts. These types, previously called "MIME Types", are now called Media Types.

The process was first defined for asynchronous mail, where limiting the number of types helps interoperability when the remote system is unknown. In new environments, where more types are no hindrance, that procedure is excessively restrictive. RFC 1590 therefore generalizes it and also covers mapping X.400 Object Identifiers (OIDs) to Media Types.
sections.eli5: The old rules for adding a new label to the list were made for email and were too strict for other uses, so this memo relaxes them.

sections.title: The Two-Step Registration Procedure
sections.content:
The RFC says plainly that this is not a formal standards process. It is an administrative procedure meant to allow community comment and sanity checking without excessive delay.

Step 1: send the proposed content-type/subtype to the ietf-types mailing list, which exists only for reviewing proposed Media Types. Proposed types are not formally registered and must use the x- notation for the subtype name. Reviewers look at the name, version references, which OIDs to use and the security considerations section.

Step 2: after two weeks, send the request and supporting documents to IANA. If a reasonable review period has passed, IANA registers the type, assigns an OID under the IANA branch and makes the registration available. Registrations are posted in an anonymous FTP directory and listed in the periodic "Assigned Numbers" RFC. The description may also be published as an Informational RFC.
sections.eli5: First you show your idea to a group and wait two weeks for comments. Then you give it to the list keeper, who writes it down officially.

sections.title: Clarifications on Four Issues
sections.content:
The RFC answers four specific complaints.

  • Limited number of types: wanting common types does not require limiting registration. Restrictions could even cause separate registration authorities with conflicting values. A recommended subset belongs in an applicability statement.
  • Published specification: naming a particular software package and version is enough when no public specification exists.
  • Security: a type need not be secure, but known risks must be identified. No exhaustive review is required.
  • Standards status: registration is not endorsement by IANA or the IETF. Becoming an Internet Standard needs the IETF process.
sections.eli5: Getting on the list does not mean anyone says your idea is good. It only means the name is taken and the known risks are written down.

sections.title: The IANA Registration Template
sections.content:
Appendix A gives an email template addressed to IANA. Its fields are the Media Type name, subtype name, required parameters, optional parameters, encoding considerations, security considerations, published specification, and a contact person with email address. If the top-level type is new, the requester must explain why an existing one cannot be used.

New top-level types are expected to be rare. Their specification must be published as an RFC, or submitted so it can become one, and be subject to the Internet standards process. In general MIME is extended by subtypes. The appendix also says new content-type parameters should not be defined as a way to introduce new functionality.
sections.eli5: It is a form with blanks: what the type is called, what extra settings it has, what the risks are and who to call with questions.

sections.title: Security and Status
sections.content:
The memo does not address specific security issues. It outlines a security review process for Media Types, carried out through the public posting and the required security considerations field.

It is Informational and updates RFC 1521. It says it does not specify an Internet standard of any kind.
sections.eli5: The memo does not fix security problems itself. It just makes sure people look for them before a label is added.
